utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to start final argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. Your Honours, just some very brief introductory points. First of all, as we usually do, I'd like to introduce Mr. Nathan Rasiah, who is sitting over to my left, who has been a member of the team over these important final stages. Ms. Butler is still with the team, but certain visa issues have turned her into a one-woman flying Dutchman, with the result that she's not currently in the Netherlands, of course. But she's still with the team. Secondly, Your Honour, very briefly, we would -- Mr. Harmon gave many thanks to all sorts of people who contributed. We would simply like, very briefly, to associate ourselves with the thanks to all the support that this Court has had from all concerned, interpreters and everybody. If I don't go through the list again, I would like it to be understood that we associate ourselves with that. And we also, in the same way that we were very pleased to hear that, we acknowledge the courtesy and professionalism from our colleagues on the Prosecution team throughout the case. Your Honours, so far as the material today is concerned, and following the discussion yesterday evening, we have on the Defence side prepared what I've called two clips. They're fairly short clips of material which will go with particular areas that I propose to explore later on this morning, but I'm not getting to those areas immediately. Those clips will, with a fair wind, be all ready when I get to that point, and for the interpreters' booth as well. But I'm not talking about anything daunting, Your Honour, I'm talking about something where it's going to be much easier for all of Your Honours and everybody else to turn to a sheet of paper rather than have to go digging around on screens and so on. Your Honours, what our final submissions are not going to be today is they are not going to be just another 30 or 40.000 words of supplement to our final brief. They are also not intended to be a repetition of our final brief. They are intended to be complementary to our final brief, but more importantly, complementary to 27.000 pages of transcript, thousands of exhibits, and about two and a half years of this trial, because this is, after all, a final submission. So, Your Honour, it's not even remotely - and how could it be? - an attempt to dig into the detail of the case, except in one or two illustrative ways. And what we've done is we've selected a couple of areas where we will go into some detail in relation to specific items, but they are selected by way of illustration and example of the -- of underlying questions in relation to the approach to the masses of material that the Trial Chamber has. So I hope it's helpful to Your Honours to know where it is this final submission is going and the sort of exercise that the Defence considers it's engaged in today. Your Honour, that doesn't mean that some very well-known aspects of a trial do not, nevertheless, justify mention and justify emphasis, because they do after the length of this trial and the mountains of material that Your Honours face now as a rather daunting task. We must acknowledge that. It's elementary, but nevertheless so important to bear in mind the burden of proof, to remember always that Mr. Krajisnik, when he was brought to The Hague - of course we know that - six years ago, he was brought here as an indicted but innocent man. He remains here today as an indicted but innocent man. That's elementary. He can only be convicted of any charge if Your Honours, or at least two of Your Honours, are satisfied that on the evidence beyond reasonable doubt his guilt is established. The English courts -- but that's just courts from one country. The English courts in modern times rephrased "beyond reasonable doubt" as that Judges or a jury, more conventionally, must be "satisfied so they are sure." But that's been confirmed as just another way, and found to be more comprehensible to a jury, more readily understandable, just another way of expressing that familiar test of beyond reasonable doubt. But it's sometime useful to have that alternative phraseology in mind. It really is sureness which is at the heart of it. The mountains of material - and they are - that Your Honours have in this case include or involve extreme variations in weight and reliability, and that is an additional difficulty that Your Honours have compared with many trial courts, by which I meaning judges or juries, wherever, because particularly where a jury is involved, there is generally much more sifting. There are quite straight gates through which evidence has to get before it can be put before those responsible for the final judgements on the evidence and on the facts, under whatever directions of law they are given or give themselves. In this particular case, the Trial Chamber, as Trial Chambers generally in this institution, have taken the view that with few exceptions material will be admitted into evidence and then it will be weighed for whatever value it has or, possibly in some cases, just does not have at all. That has produced an enormous quantity of material for the parties, of course, but now, over however long it is between now and the day of Your Honours' judgement, that is a daunting aspect of an already daunting task. There has been - and this is a Defence submission - without going over the motions which we have fought and lost - we haven't lost every motion on the Defence side, I'm very pleased to say; we have occasionally succeeded - but we have, of course, in the course of this trial launched a number of motions in relation to timing, scheduling, calling of evidence, and it wouldn't be unfair to say that we have generally not been conspicuously successful in obtaining what we sought by those motions. But what's not appropriate is for us now today, in these submissions, to be refighting or relaunching those motions. We don't propose to do that. Subject to all appeal procedures which we have or haven't been able to exhaust or which might lie ahead, those are decisions and those are, as they stand, binding, and some of them will be binding forever. But it still leaves Your Honours with heavy difficulties in fairly weighing the evidence, because it would remain our submission, consistent with what I have just said, that the course of this case has produced some significant imbalances. We started with, in many instances, protracted evidence of Prosecution witnesses. And when I say "protracted" I'm not necessarily implying any serious criticism of anybody, no, nor am I necessarily throwing aside any possibility of criticism of anybody in relation to that exercise. It doesn't really matter to explore that particular issue. But a number of Prosecution witnesses gave evidence over really what in retrospect was quite a long time, and when one looks at the many, many days spent with some of the Prosecution witnesses, then one looks at the really quite severe compression of time that was imposed in relation to some of the later and, on the face of it, very important Prosecution witnesses; and then one looks at the, in some cases, very severe compression of time which was imposed in relation to Defence witnesses, and then when one comes on to what in the Defence's submission is and was a really extraordinary and - we don't shrink from the words - sometimes frankly farcical compression of time in relation to Chamber's witnesses, the weighing of all the evidence in this case must bear those considerations in mind. Look at Mr. Mandic's evidence. I don't mean look at it here and now, line by line. Look at the number of days over which Mr. Mandic gave evidence. Look at the number of hours over which Mrs. Plavsic gave evidence. Just an example. We reinforce and endorse the invitation from the Prosecution to scrutinise all the material in this case in great detail. We have no fears or concerns on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf from the most detailed scrutiny of the material which is manageable for Your Honours. In the circumstances of this case, it's liable to be dangerously unfair to the Defence if there is any compromise in that work. The Prosecution case has been supported by a welter of detail. It's not all good detail; it's not all useful detail. But it's indisputably detail. But it has also been in some ways painted, the picture that the Prosecution has drawn and painted, has been in some respect painted with crude, primitive lines and simple primary colours. This was a brutal civil war; that's clear. That, so far as evidence was required to back up what everybody in fact knew when we arrived in court, but in the end evidence is important, of course, the critically important thing, that was apparent from the very first witness from the very first day from the very first days of the trial. We have never challenged on Mr. Krajisnik's behalf, he has never asked us to challenge the proposition that this brutal civil war led to terrible crimes committed in many parts of former Yugoslavia, tragically, but particularly, of course, we are concerned with Bosnia. That's indisputable. Serbs against Muslims and Croats, not part of the charges in this case. Terrible crimes committed by members of all those ethnic groups, but it is Mr. Krajisnik who is on trial. There was, and we have seen many instances, there was extreme language used by participants in these terrible events. Some of the most extreme was actually used by Chamber witness Mrs. Plavsic. Of course there was, and we would be foolish to deny it, there was much extreme language used both publicly and privately by Mr. Karadzic. And dotted -- perhaps more than dotted, but throughout much of the public record, Assembly sessions of the Serb Republic, we see very strong stuff. And no doubt if we looked all over the public record of what people were saying all over the former Yugoslavia at that time, we would see thousands and thousands and thousands of statements which normally we would never hope to see, or hope never to see. There were killings, there were rapes, there were tortures. There's much undisputed evidence. Mr. Krajisnik was one of the Bosnian Serb leaders. We've never disputed that. How could we? He held two major positions, if we can label them positions. His first and obvious position, and it was his main position - that's really the key point - he was the president of the Assembly, as he had been, and there was an overlapping period, of course, as he had been the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, both before the crisis and split in October, 1991, and for some time afterwards, although the practical aspect of that position, of course, faded away quite quickly in the circumstances. That was number one. And secondly, he was, throughout all the relevant period that we're talking about, a member of the international negotiating team - I label it that way - for the Bosnian Serbs. That is simple, as far as it goes, though each of those positions -- I'm not ignoring -- I'm not mentioning specifically at the moment, but I'm not ignoring the fact that of course he had other functions and positions. We know all that. That's on the evidence and has been explored in detail. But each of those two positions that I've mentioned, president of the Assembly and member of the international negotiating team, has its own complexities and lack of clarity in many ways. But it isn't as simple as you look at speeches of Dr. Karadzic, you see the ways in which Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were close. And they were. They knew each other. They had been involved in previous events in all sorts of different ways that the Trial Chamber has seen. So of course we don't contest that simple bare proposition. That would be foolish as well. But you've got all those inflammatory speeches; you've got an enormous crisis that developed in October, 1991. You've got arming on all sides as the spectre of civil war, imminent civil war, became more and more real. You had outbreak of increasingly extreme violence at the end of March, beginning of April, 1992, and over the ensuing months. And throughout that period, Mr. Krajisnik was, as a bare, simple label, part of the overall Bosnian Serb leadership. But a definition and a label BSL appearing here, there, in the next paragraph, and so on throughout the Prosecution final brief, doesn't tell the story, because the more you examine the evidence, the more question marks it raises and the more doubts it raises and the more complex the position appears. Far from the very basic simple picture. And we have in mind in these submissions the sort of evidence which we found in the early months of this trial, and then occasionally after that, where a witness who had no direct knowledge, no direct connection with the Bosnian Serb leadership, being asked to rank the leaders in order of importance. Some of that evidence, we suggest, is pretty much on a par with sending a journalist out into the street to ask the first 30 people whether they think X is more likely to be the next leader of the Labour Party in the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister when Mr. Blair retires, or similar in other countries. That probably - we suggest probably - Your Honours won't really have any serious difficulty in brushing aside that sort of evidence as not really helping anybody, because facts are only really useful if they're coming from somebody who actually knows something or knows enough about it for their view of the facts, or an opinion which represents some facts, to be valuable. And as a general proposition, applying to expert evidence as well as to opinions elicited from factual witnesses, but particularly perhaps in the context of this bit of our submissions, when one is talking about factual witnesses, opinions elicited from factual witnesses, even leaving aside when they have been elicited by leading questions, but opinions elicited from factual witnesses are only of any value if one can really look and see if that witness actually knows some facts, and knows some reliable facts which support that opinion. I'm not going to go delving into the transcript on this, Your Honour, nor am I shirking it. There are 27.000 pages of transcript there, and we could take all day on this point, so I won't. Mr. Krajisnik -- and this was, broadly speaking, not the usual feature. These cases vary, and we are only concerned in the end with this one. But Mr. Krajisnik gave evidence. Lots of defendants don't, after all. Obviously, Mr. Krajisnik's overall position, including the positions that I mentioned a few minutes ago - president of the Assembly, member of the international negotiating team - but his other roles, his other participation in the events of 1991 and 1992, they obviously raise questions. It would be ludicrous to suggest they don't raise questions. After all, what are we doing here? Mr. Krajisnik could see that. Mr. Krajisnik could not be so naive as to suppose that his part in all these events and the complexity, and the chaos as well of many of the events of that time, wouldn't leave him with lots of explaining to do. Of course there he was in Pale. He was personally close to Karadzic. He was highly respected in the SDS and among the Bosnian Serbs, as he had been as president of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly. Practically nobody could have come out of this war and any serious part in it, have exposed themselves to 40 days of searching evidence, including nearly three weeks of cross-examination, and ended up leaving no questions, no doubts, no incomplete explanations. It's implicit in the Trial Chamber's imposition of cut-offs on both parties, witnesses' examinations, and on Your Honours yourselves. You've imposed cut-offs and guillotines on your own participation in this trial. And in principle, although we have had plenty of tussles about that particular aspect of the case, the basic principle that a case can't go on forever and you can't explore everything right to the bitter end and down every alleyway. Of course we accept that. But it has the result that a trial arising out of such complex and fast-moving and, inevitably in wartime, chaotic events can never tie down all the complexities, can never deal with all the questions, is always going to leave unanswered, unresolved mysteries, such as why nobody ever seems to have interviewed Mr. Djeric before he got here. Strange, but there it is. So despite the phrase "search for the truth," it remains every defendant's right - not exercised by Mr. Krajisnik in this case, of course - every defendant's right to say nothing and not to face that personal scrutiny, and hide behind the burden of proof. Legitimately, of course, it's not hiding, except -- and we're not talking about this case, after all, we're talking about a case where a defendant doesn't give evidence. Again a crude view of that can sometimes be that the defendant is hiding in some way. But Mr. Krajisnik didn't even do that. It's important to remember that right from the outset Mr. Krajisnik said he would give evidence. I can't remember exactly how early in the trial it was said, but it was very early anyway. I said it on his behalf as, on this point, I was instructed to do, because it's a major element of the Defence. It's not a question of the day-to-day running of the case. That's a major element of the case on which counsel represents his client and follows his client's instructions. He never resiled from that. There were issues about timing, quite big issues about timing, and there was a point at which the Trial Chamber was saying to Mr. Krajisnik, If you're going to give evidence at all, it's going to be now. And he did. But at that point never once was there any reluctance expressed by Mr. Krajisnik or through Mr. Josse and myself on his behalf to give evidence, to subject himself to what was bound to be a very extensive and lengthy and, it can be said, inevitably extremely exhausting scrutiny. He wasn't waiting to see which way the wind was blowing. He wasn't waiting to take a major tactical decision or strategic decision, however one labels it, whether, in light of the Prosecution evidence, the downside was worth the upside, whether the risks of going in the box were less than the risks of not going in the box, and so on. Those are legitimate decisions, legitimate considerations for a defendant to weigh and be advised upon and make decisions upon. It's just that it didn't arise here. Mr. Krajisnik was always determined to give his account of these events, give his part of it, and be interrogated. And I mean interrogated in the proper and legitimate way that interrogation in court is done. And he wasn't asking for any limit. He, and we on his behalf, were prepared for him to be exposed to that, with whatever limits of time the Trial Chamber chose to impose or not impose. And inevitably, even with 40 days of evidence, inevitably there were enormous chunks of the case and numerous points in the evidence that it was just completely unrealistic to expect us, any of us, to have been able to explore with Mr. Krajisnik. So that doesn't answer the charges, of course. That's -- we have to look at all the evidence for that. But it does cast light on Mr. Krajisnik's character then and now, which is material, and his wish to tell the truth. After all, he knows -- well, he would be a far less intelligent and perspicacious man than he obviously is. He knows that once you put yourself in the witness box and once you subject yourself to experienced professional cross-examination - leave aside examination-in-chief - once you expose yourself to experienced professional cross-examination in front of an experienced Bench of professional Judges in an international criminal court, it's not so easy to hide the truth. That's clear. Everybody -- we're not talking about the Defence team here -- everybody concerned is easily good enough at their job for that to be Mr. Krajisnik's position and for him to have been able to see that. Mr. Harmon -- I think it was Mr. Harmon. There was some changing around yesterday but I think it was him for this particular bit. Mr. Harmon, as is his job, he launched into Mr. Krajisnik's credibility yesterday. We can understand, Mr. Krajisnik can understand, that's what Mr. Harmon would do. The Trial Chamber will weigh the content, all the evidence and Mr. Krajisnik's, the gravity of the charges, the accusations and the evidential points which in the course of the case have been shown to be unfair or unfounded. That's bound to happen. Again, I'm not suggesting that in a case of this size and complexity, the Prosecution is not going to find among the hundreds - hundreds - thousands of allegations they make, some are going to collapse and end up in dust. The same is going to happen on the Defence side. Not everything ends up, at the end of the trial, as either party suggests. But it's part of the examination and it's part of the evidence of Mr. Krajisnik that the man giving evidence -- I'm talking particularly about Mr. Krajisnik now and not talking about other witnesses for the moment. He's defending himself -- well, through us, he's defending himself against the gravest charges there are. He is having, again understandably, legitimately in a trial of this nature, he's having accusations put to him which are outrageous to him in many instances, and in a number of instances are clearly not right in the nature of things. So in the course of 40 days of evidence, realistically there's going to be a wide variation in the tenor of the evidence, the tenor -- the balance of the answers. Some answers from somebody in Mr. Krajisnik's position are going to be clearly correct. Some are going to be utterly convincing. At the other end of the spectrum, it would be astonishing if in the course of 40 days of evidence, any witness for practical purposes, but certainly any defendant who exposes himself to give evidence, isn't going to give some answers which the Trial Chamber won't swallow. That's normal. It would be an extraordinary trial if that didn't happen. Now, of course, what's important is how big the questions are, how big the answers are on those particular points. That's another matter. But we would endorse and concur with our learned friends on the Prosecution side in a number of simple approaches to the case, not surprisingly, because we do similar jobs in our very different ways on the different sides of the courtroom. The evaluation of any witness's evidence is not an all-or-nothing exercise, except in the rarest cases. I'm paraphrasing and probably not so elegantly expressing what Mr. Harmon said yesterday. But you don't look at a witness's evidence usually and say, Well, I don't believe a single word of it, or a witness's evidence and say, I accept absolutely everything that that witness says. Many witnesses, there's going to be a combination of true and false. Nearly all witnesses, if there's not some combination of true and false, there's a combination of right and wrong in the sense that their description really isn't an apt description. They come infected by their own, sometimes inevitable, human deficiencies in memory after many years, particular personal feelings and convictions about the events concerned. It's a complex exercise in relation to Mr. Krajisnik himself, for the reasons I've just summarised. They are familiar to Your Honours, but not everything which is already familiar to Your Honours is therefore not worth saying today. It's a complex exercise, particularly in relation to Mr. Krajisnik's evidence, but more widely. I've used the phrase "search for the truth" because it's been used quite a lot in the course of this trial. If you do a LiveNote search, a guess would be that the first person to use the phrase was Your Honour Judge Orie, but it doesn't matter because the phrase has been used on a number of occasions. And it was used yesterday in the Prosecution's submissions, particularly in the part of Mr. Harmon's submissions where he was rejecting the Defence suggestion that it was not quite what the Prosecution was doing. That was where it particularly came up. It's not the slightest impugning of professionalism of the Prosecution to persist with our contention that of course they're not quite doing that. But neither, in the fullest sense, does a trial. There are real dangers in the label "search for the truth" applied to a time-limited adversarial trial. Time-limited is inevitable in this world, but adversarial trial of this nature. It's -- of course the hope and intention is that any trial gets as near to the truth as can be achieved. That's the hope of the Trial Chamber. That's the hope of the -- when I say the international community, I mean the international human community - I mean everybody - that that's, as far as possible, what happens. But it isn't quite like that after all. It is, in the end, a search to see if the Prosecution have proved their allegations on all the evidence. If there is a difference - and sometimes there may be - if there is a difference between that and the fullest finding of the truth, well, we go back to that description of what we're doing. It is a search to see if the Prosecution have proved their allegations on all the evidence. And they have had a lot more help -- or Your Honours have had a lot more help in bringing that nearer to a search for the truth in this case by the fact that Mr. Krajisnik has courageously and persistently from the beginning said that he would, and has in the end, said that he would give and has given evidence himself. What it means by saying that it's a search to see if the Prosecution have proved their allegations on all the evidence is that it is, on the one hand, improper to speculate, to plug gaps in the Prosecution case, and secondly, that it is an essential requirement to allow properly for the evidence being incomplete wherever that casts any doubt. I'm not sure that's brilliantly phrased, that last point, so I'll have another go. Because the exercise is of its nature incomplete, it ties in with the essential nature of the exercise and the fundamental burden of proof. Wherever there is any issue which it hasn't been possible to resolve, it hasn't been possible to explore fully, it hasn't been possible to obtain full evidence or, in some cases, the evidence that one would reasonably wish to see if there were more time and had been more resources, wherever it's not possible to complete the exercise, the gaps can only be plugged where it's absolutely clear how the -- first of all, they can be plugged and, secondly, how they would be plugged. What would fit in there? If what fits in is just something obvious from the real world, and bits of evidence, A, B, C, lead inevitably to a reliable, sure inference that you've got D as well, put them together. No problem. But if you've got A, B, C and we didn't get on to the further questions and there is any possibility that the correct answer would be either D or E or F or G, then in every case of course the most favourable assumption has to be made for the defendant, because that's an obvious and logical corollary of it being impossible to be sure about any of those alternatives. So where questions don't have crystal clear answers - I'm using "crystal clear" as a broad synonym for "beyond reasonable doubt." Sure, beyond reasonable doubt, crystal clear; Your Honours know what the test is ultimately. Wherever questions don't have crystal clear answers, so far as they're material questions, of course they simply have to be treated in the most favourable way to Mr. Krajisnik. That's what the burden and the standard of proof mean. And he remains innocent and he is not guilty unless the charges are made good to a level of sureness on the evidence. Let's look at the important issue of quality of evidence. I'm not going through 120 witnesses, being here until December, going through the transcript, but looking at the important lines on the issue of quality of evidence. We did highlight some categories in the final brief. You've got to have categories; otherwise, we're going to be going through 120-something of them. We won't repeat either the categories in detail or the points and submissions in the final brief. But, summarising, we say that careful evaluation, of course of each witness, that goes without saying -- though there are some witnesses whose evidence is not seriously in dispute. That's a different issue. The one immediately springs to mind I can't name anyway because that was a protected witness, but Your Honours will be familiar with some of the witnesses who came and gave evidence of the terrible things that had happened in their locality to their families, and it was truly awful in many cases. And those things happened, in many cases clearly happened. In some cases, perhaps there's some fault of recollection, exaggeration. In many cases that's just entirely human and in many cases it doesn't matter. Your Honours will -- I mean the fault of recollection doesn't matter. The events themselves will always matter, of course. Your Honours can evaluate all that. But when we come to the quite significant number of witnesses who -- well, were either fortunate enough not to suffer directly personally, although in many cases their own families had suffered somewhere, but the ones who were coming not to give evidence about the specific crimes but other issues in the case, they do require, as categories, some attention to the elements of the category. But then, obviously, the individual witnesses are and the individual evidence is what really has to be examined. With international witnesses, we don't say that any of the international witnesses started off hostile to Serbs sometime before the -- even the events with which this case is concerned. We don't say that. And we certainly don't say there's any sort of inherent ethnic hostility. That would be absurd. We don't suggest that. But we do say simply that close involvement in events such as these can lead to strong but sometimes wrong views and judgements and clouded recollections of events. And that can be because anybody's involvement, and sometimes especially because they have involvement which is very close to the events which is there on the ground, anybody's involvement then is likely to be necessarily selective. It's localised. They have their own particular responsibilities. They are involved in particular actions. Some of the international witnesses, it was part of their job to see the broad picture and the big picture. But everybody's human and, for example, we have identified -- and I won't repeat it, it's there in our final brief, but we have identified a passage in Mr. Okun's evidence where, for all he's acknowledged - tremendous distinction, no question about that - the answer he gives is just unconvincing. His explanation of a particular well-known pronouncement by Mr. Izetbegovic can't be right. So the Court must proceed on, and only on, the clear facts about Mr. Krajisnik and then only such opinions and judgements as are really solid so that you, Your Honours, can be sure about them. And Your Honours, we hope and trust, will always be wary of facts, because that's a hard enough evaluation to make in many instances, but will be especially wary, we ask, throughout the case and throughout Your Honours' review of the material of opinions and judgements. We do suggest that there are and were witnesses clearly hostile to Mr. Krajisnik, and again we urge Your Honours to evaluate that evidence carefully and have that in mind. Again, we don't put forward the unrealistic proposition that because a witness is hostile, that witness is lying, or because a witness is particularly hostile about Mr. Krajisnik, that what they say about Mr. Krajisnik is false. The Defence case doesn't involve, we hope, such crude propositions. But it does involve the greatest care. And we do suggest that you will find, from time to time in the course of Mr. Kljuic's evidence, for example, a clear hostility to Mr. Krajisnik. Now, the events at that time and Mr. Kljuic's own role, and what happened to Mr. Kljuic will have fuelled some of that. And it's not the issue for Your Honours' judgement as to how much of that hostility is justified, how much of that hostility is unjustified. That's a case within a case within a case. And in the end, some of that is for Mr. Kljuic to resolve perhaps. But it's there and we do say -- we do, I think, in the course of the morning, will come to a particular point in the illustrative material which we've put before Your Honours. And if we don't, then I've not remembered what it is I'm going to be saying in the course of this morning, but I think we get to. So I'll pass on from Mr. Kljuic. The same applies to Mr. Bjelobrk. The interesting thing about Mr. Bjelobrk really is that Mr. Krajisnik -- and he expressed this: Mr. Krajisnik clearly retains some respect, real respect, for Mr. Bjelobrk. He acknowledged that. But that doesn't mean that Mr. Bjelobrk is right. And in the end, it's not -- Your Honours sometimes in this case, and of course perhaps not that infrequently, but sometimes in the case Your Honours will see witnesses that in Your Honours' judgement are simply not telling the truth. Well, we've identified one that we say falls into that category, but there are others. And the Prosecution, of course, identify lots as well. That's obviously a feature of this trial. But lots of witnesses on lots of points are just wrong. Fine line sometimes between untruthful and wrong; sometimes it's not necessary for a court to make a decision on that line. Ultimately it may not matter on a particular point. What matters is whether that piece of evidence is sufficiently safe, sufficiently sure, to be accepted by the Trial Chamber, and sometimes it can be rejected as not sufficiently reliable without actually deciding whether it's deliberately untruthful, it's reckless, it's mistaken, and so on. But they are not the only witnesses where we -- there are degrees of hostility as well, after all. They are not the only witnesses where we see that. And even justified hostility, if it may be, and that's a matter of judgement -- also it's a matter of strong feelings sometimes of the witness himself, that he feels justified about that, and from his perspective and what he knows and what he remembers, there may be a justification. Even if everybody knew everything, there wouldn't be. But nobody knows that. But it's real, justified or unjustified, if there is animosity, hostility, it's to be weighed in the balance. Not in the crude way that I disavowed a few minutes ago, but importantly. And then, well, special category, she's really a special category all on her own: Mrs. Plavsic. She's a special category on her own in lots of ways. But hostility to Mr. Krajisnik, she's certainly in a league of her own, it seems, as far as that's concerned. I'll come back to Mrs. Plavsic. Those are just three witnesses, degrees of hostility there, especially now I've mentioned the last of those. Then there's the category -- not a category named in this way in our final brief, but a different way of looking at it: Witnesses clearly worried about their own position. It largely embraces the convicts and the suspects. Some suspects never became convicts. All convicts presumably were once suspects. The witnesses clearly worried about their own position, for one reason or another, would have included Mr. Mandic, Mr. Djeric, Mr. Trbojevic, Mr. Babic. It doesn't end there, but those are clear examples. For one reason or another; slightly different reasons, perhaps. Mr. Mandic, well, he might have been even more worried now than he was then, if policies and practices and public pronouncements haven't moved on in this Tribunal, because there's Mr. Mandic identified in the latest version of the JCE, hot off the press from the OTP in this case, as one of the core members - or is it members of the core JCE? But if the Prosecution are driven, as actually they absolutely have to be from their grand compendious super JCE, as listed in the original indictment to their contention that we're talking about a hard-core JCE - my phrase, not theirs - it includes Mr. Mandic in their list. Mr. Mandic, from the Defence's recollection, was giving evidence just a matter of days or weeks before the shutters were going to come down or go up on further indictments in this Tribunal. But he had given -- he had been interviewed; he'd said a lot of things in his interview. Mr. Mandic's personality perhaps doesn't lead him to betray obvious signs of anxiety and worry because he seemed to be an ebullient, resilient personality. But on the assumption - and it's a hundred per cent reliable assumption - there was plenty going on in Mr. Mandic's head, he would have been a worried man. Mr. Djeric, well, how much he's been quietly worrying down there in Bosnia over the years in which he's been largely left to himself is a question, but he was the Prime Minister throughout all the key events of 1992 -- well, certainly for the key months of 1992. He was, by the Prosecution lights, a member of the expanded Presidency. There is still rather a question whether that really is Mr. Djeric's view despite the snapshot summary of his evidence given yesterday by the Prosecution. But it would be enough to make a person worried, wouldn't it, if Mr. Krajisnik is on trial with a key feature of the case against him being his membership in the expanded Presidency and Mr. Djeric himself, by the same token, would have been just that thing. Mr. Trbojevic. Odd position, Mr. Trbojevic, since apparently once upon a time he was wanting to sit where Mr. Josse is sitting, but a professional lawyer, it wouldn't take much to knock that career off course, would it, given that he was the Deputy Prime Minister at the time. Mr. Babic. I'm just going to mention Mr. Babic, Your Honour. He had his reasons. When he gave evidence, he had his reasons to be worried. New category: Witnesses who it would be naive to suppose would take an acquittal of Mr. Krajisnik lightly as a matter of no concern to them. And I want -- well, I want all my submissions to be clearly understood, and if they're not, well, it could sometimes be because they are not clearly expressed, no doubt. But this one relates to or is a development of what we say in our final brief in relation to such witnesses as Mr. Treanor, Ms. Hanson, Mr. Nielsen, Mr. Wilson, Mr. Brown; all honourable men and lady. I don't want to sound like Marc Antony, but all honourable people. We don't suggest anything different. But particularly in the cases of Mr. Treanor, Ms. Hanson, Mr. Nielsen, they have contributed hundreds of hours of work to a team of which they were members, and it would be ridiculous not broadly to accept and acknowledge that Treanor, Hanson and Nielsen are members of the Prosecution team overall. What do they want out of this case? They want a conviction. And it's not -- I don't mean that Mr. Treanor would come here and make things up because he got some preconceived clear idea that Mr. Krajisnik was guilty. I'm not suggesting it's like when the police stitch somebody up in the police station because they should have got him for the last one and they want to make sure they get him for this one. That sort of thing happens around the world. Less and less, we hope. Nothing like that. Of course nothing like that. But careful evaluation, it's our point, how independent or not independent is an expert. Is an expert working to a thesis? That's really what it comes to. And it's all right up to a point, as long as everybody recognises that that's what they're doing. The problems, if you like, and the dangers and the risks involved in that and the slightly unusual status and position of expert -- Prosecution expert witnesses in this Tribunal compared with what many of us are used to, and I don't know exactly what people are used to in other places, but I rather do suggest that almost everywhere it's something at least different from what we see in this Tribunal, it's just an extra task - big one, tough one - it's just an extra task for Your Honours. It just means that all their evidence has to be scrutinised and evaluated with that in mind; that you need, with respect, then, to be super alert to -- Your Honours would be super alert all the time, but super, super alert, to the risk that there is a thesis that the most scrupulous researcher - Mr. Treanor is a researcher - the most scrupulous researcher has to -- the most scrupulous application of scientific method, people really have to struggle to stop themselves from putting together material to fit their own thesis. And as long as Your Honours are alert always to that aspect of the process, ultimately no harm should or would be done. But that's what's important. And possibly to a lesser degree, but we leave that to Your Honours to evaluate, the same would apply to Mr. Wilson, Mr. Brown. But Treanor, Hanson, Nielsen, that's massive material; footnote upon footnote, appendix upon appendix, and it all has to be viewed in that light, with that extra care. Chambers' witnesses, a slightly different type of category, if I can put it that way, from the way in which we have broken it down in the final brief. But then this is complementary to that brief and not just a plug-in. Chambers' witnesses, one word applies very aptly to the Chambers' witnesses as a group and their evidence as a whole, and that word is "extraordinary." Mrs. Plavsic. I said I would come back to Mrs. Plavsic. Mrs. Plavsic, she's come up before, of course. Excuse me one moment, Your Honour. She's perhaps travelled more often from Sweden to The Hague than she's given evidence in The Hague. But in the Stakic trial, the Trial Chamber noted this, and it's paragraph 550 of the Stakic trial judgement: "Ultimately, the Trial Chamber decided that there was no point in postponing the end of the hearings in the case in order to hear Plavsic, because without anticipating her testimony, it could not reasonably be expected that having pleaded guilty to persecution and not genocide she could or would make any statement that would lead the Trial Chamber to the conclusion that any person mentioned in the indictment had the specific intent." Well, "mentioned in the indictment" -- I haven't double-checked, I expect Mr. Krajisnik is mentioned in the indictment in the Stakic case. But what the Trial Chamber fondly supposed there in paragraph 550 would perhaps require a certain amount of revisiting. But be that as it may, that's not the key point. The point is this: That we -- Mrs. Plavsic is a convicted war criminal by reason of her own plea. That's indisputable. The one thing we can't argue with here is that she is convicted. She pleaded. She signed up to a factual basis for her plea, so that was her saying, Yes, I accept this. And on the basis of what she signed up to, what she specifically agreed, what she specifically accepted, she was convicted of persecution and sent to prison. So she's a convicted war criminal. Mr. Harmon yesterday, page 18 of the LiveNote transcript, line 1 or 2, I think: "Beyond the excerpt from her statement just cited -" that's Mrs. Plavsic - "in her statement she directed the Court to sections of her book that she considered relevant to Mr. Krajisnik. In court she testified that, 'I wrote there that the name of the book is very binding, as far as I'm concerned. That's why I call the book "I Testify." And I said it as if I had given an oath that I would speak the truth, only the truth, so help me God. And that's what also kept, like a thread, appearing throughout this book and also the second book.'" Fine words. It's only that perhaps in evaluating Mrs. Plavsic's words and the help that she implores from God and the oath that she would speak the truth, perhaps the fact that she doesn't actually acknowledge in her books what she's pleaded guilty to before this Tribunal might just be tossed into the balance somewhere. You wouldn't let Mrs. Plavsic's hands anywhere near the handle of the sword of justice, would you? And if we -- well, "we" is really Your Honours. If we had wished to embark and actually carry out the exercise of thoroughly exploring Mrs. Plavsic's acknowledged crimes, her acknowledged -- overtly acknowledged hostility to Mr. Krajisnik, her blatant hypocritical untruth, to get to the bottom of all that, we'd have needed rather longer than the little cameo to which Mrs. Plavsic was subjected and in which she participated in this court at the very end of this trial. It's worthless rubbish, Mrs. Plavsic's evidence. Page 75 of yesterday's LiveNote transcript, Mr. Harmon: "Mr. Krajisnik was part of a criminal enterprise." That's line 23 or 24, I think. "Mr. Krajisnik was part of a criminal enterprise. The persons who were close to him and were also engaged in the enterprise and were convicted of crimes related to the enterprise are ideally the persons who are likely to know information and have evidence that's vital to the search for the truth." Well, if I say those are fine words from Mr. Harmon, of course I'm not going to say about Mr. Harmon's fine words the very things I said about Mr. Plavsic's fine words. They are different categories, of course. But in their different way, for very different reasons, of course. Mr. Harmon's fine words don't really bear more than a few seconds scrutiny either. Who were these people related to the enterprise who were ideally the persons who were likely to know information, have evidence that's vital to the search for the truth? Well, they didn't call Mrs. Plavsic. They didn't call Mr. Subotic. They didn't call Mr. Ostojic. They didn't even interview or apparently trouble, Mr. Djeric. We didn't get a sniff of Mr. Buha being called by the Prosecution. They didn't suggest bringing Mr. Maksimovic here. And where was Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Mico Stanisic? Well, maybe not so far away, maybe not so inaccessible. It's just not so, is it? It's not untruthful. We're not talking about a witness being brought from Sweden. We're talking about professional lead counsel putting his case. But it just doesn't work, that proposition. It just demonstrates, and that brief list I've given just demonstrates that this search for the truth can be quite heavily qualified. I've mentioned Mr. Djeric before. It's not surprising that he tries to shuffle everything from the government to the Presidency, because actually he doesn't really -- he doesn't really regard himself as a member of the Presidency, so that when he shuffles things off from the government to the Presidency, he's not actually sitting there in this court saying, I, as the head of the government, actually wasn't responsible for this, this is really the responsibility of the Presidency which, oh, whoops, by the way, I was also a member. He's not doing that. He's actually saying, I was government, but that Presidency over there, they were the ones who knew all this and what was going on, and, well, we were sort in the dark over where we were. Mr. Ostojic. Well, probably nobody is going to make the unsullied truthfulness of Mr. Ostojic the central plank of their case, either Prosecution or Defence, so once again we have an area of happy or unhappy agreement between us there. But, again, you don't normally accept or reject any witness's evidence wholesale, and Mr. Ostojic, he was certainly there, and how. Mr. Deronjic, apart from -- it's a big apart, of course, but apart from the early witnesses who came to tell us about the crimes on the ground in their municipality, Mr. Gasi, the very first witness, but very soon after, Mr. Deronjic was first up as a big witness, if you like. No disrespect to Mr. Gasi, but in the overall scheme of this case. First up as a big witness. Quite big pressure to get Mr. Deronjic on and done and dusted in this case before he was, well, seriously dealt with in his own case. He committed an appalling crime. We know that. He committed an appalling crime. He can't complain -- maybe he did complain about the sentence he got for that. He torched a village and murdered 60 people, something like that. He says he went to Pale the next day. If it wasn't the next day -- I think I remember it was the next day, but anyway it was extremely soon after, he says. And he told a meeting what had happened in Bratunac, which Glogova is included. Well, I'm not going to pick and pore over Mr. Deronjic's evidence here this morning because, well, Your Honours can do that in the quietness of your own chambers and see how unsatisfactory Mr. Deronjic's evidence is if you simply look at it on its own -- well, on its own in the context without looking at what other witnesses have said about it. Was Mr. Deronjic telling the truth in court? Big question. Was Mr. Deronjic telling the truth -- well, if Mr. Deronjic is basically telling the truth about the meeting that he went to in Pale and the people who were there and what he talked about, if that happened in that way, was he telling the truth at that meeting? Even bigger question. Most unlikely. Most -- most unlikely that he was really telling the truth about everything he had done. At that time and in those circumstances, the notion that however strong the feelings that were riding high, exactly what we know Mr. Deronjic now did was a subject of boasting and bursts of applause, that really is a bit far-fetched. And then what he did actually tell the meeting, if he did. Did he tell them what was then inevitably passed on to Mr. Krajisnik? Does the combination of what Mr. Deronjic says about that meeting and what he had to hide and where he was when he came to give it -- where he was metaphorically when he came to give evidence in this court, does that really lead to any reliable conclusion that Mr. Krajisnik himself knew immediately after those events of criminal actions sufficiently serious to pin criminal liability on him here? Of course it's important to the Prosecution. Naturally they want to -- they want to get in as early in time as they can and get as clearly as they can Mr. Krajisnik's knowledge of such matters. It's just it's pretty thin stuff on which to base that. When -- Mr. Ostojic, of course, was specifically named and, well, graphically and in colour, as it were, in the colour blue by Mr. Deronjic as somebody at that meeting. When the Trial Chamber - I think this must have been Your Honour Judge Orie - was summarising his statement, 3rd of July, this year. But transcript -- we needn't go to it, I'm sure Your Honours can find it, but transcript 26637, a summary by Trial Chamber: "You --" that's Mr. Ostojic. "You did not recall an alleged attack on the village of Glogova on the 9th of May, 1992. You stated that you were not present at an alleged meeting in Pale of SDS Crisis Staffs and municipality presidents around the 10th of May, 1992, and you denied the allegation that you chaired such a meeting with Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic and even expressed doubt that such a meeting even took place. You remembered that you and General Mladic attended a meeting in the beginning of May 1992.". Mr. Harmon cross-examined the following day. It's a short passage, Your Honour, so I haven't distributed bits of the transcript. But Your Honour can find it, certainly, at 26742, on the 4th of July, 2006. For various practical reasons, the cross-examination proceeded initially on this point rather less smoothly than we're accustomed to when Mr. Harmon is examining a witness. There were hitches in the course of this. But at page 26743, there had been a slip of the tongue about where the meeting had taken place. Line 23, Your Honour Judge Orie: "Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Harmon made a mistake when he said you did attend the meeting in Glogova -" that had just been a slip of the tongue - "on the 10th of May and that you used the map, et cetera. You said: 'No, I did not attend the meeting on the 10th of May in Glogova' because you were in Pale. Did you attend that meeting in Pale of which --" and then the witness answered: "No, no. On the 10th of May I was in the Pale in the government, and I was drafting the law on the Ministry of Information for the following session of the government which was to take place on the 12th of May in Banja Luka. And already on the 11th of May I was on my way to Banja Luka." Your Honour Judge Orie: "Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. We'll have a break."
